project.description: Static review of the source tree trezor-vendored-crypto at 72489948b3c44a37598de9da658be28e4fabb4ae. 519 files analysed; of 1159 files, 174 are test, fuzzing, benchmark or example code and were left out, 466 are not read by any analyzer, 0 exceed the per-file limit and 0 did not fit the total limit. 519 files come from directories a .gitmodules pins and are read as shipped source rather than skipped as a dependency cache. No requests were sent to the owner's systems.

decisions.note: Correct, and the count needs reading carefully rather than quoting. 94 rows is one per file of the *complete* upstream SPHINCS+ reference implementation, which this submodule is: four backends — ref/, haraka-aesni/, sha2-avx2/, shake-a64/, shake-avx2/ — and 18 parameter-set headers under ref/params/. A Trezor's microcontroller cannot execute the AVX2 or AArch64 SIMD code at all, and the build compiles exactly one parameter set, so the honest statement about the device is not "94 implementations of SLH-DSA" but "Trezor pins the whole SPHINCS+ reference implementation and compiles one configuration from it" — which is much stronger evidence of real migration work than an imported header, and is where the main audit's boot_header.c:30 call site leads. 17 of the 94 rows are the Haraka instantiation, which FIPS 205 did *not* standardise (it covers the SHA2 and SHAKE instantiations), so those rows are pre-standard SPHINCS+ rather than SLH-DSA proper; they are upstream's and say nothing about what Trezor selected. Kept at the detector's medium confidence. This is also the finding that proves the detector was wrong before today: the previous run read these same 123 files and reported zero SLH-DSA rows, because the reference implementation calls itself SPX_* and spx_ctx and never writes the standard's name.

Correct: 24 files of vendor/secp256k1-zkp, Blockstream's fork of libsecp256k1, which is what a Trezor actually signs Bitcoin transactions with. The main audit's 73 Shor-breakable rows count the call sites in core/embed/sec; these are the implementation under them. The two should be read together and not added together — it is one dependency measured at two levels, which is why this bundle is not folded into the portfolio's per-codebase counts.
Correct, four files, the schnorrsig module of the same vendored library: Taproot spends.

Correct and directly relevant to the migration story rather than to spending. Ed25519 is what the device's boot header is signed with today — core/embed/sec/image/boot_header.c:81 in the main audit — and these five rows are its implementation. This is the primitive SLH-DSA is being added alongside, so the pair Ed25519-plus-SLH-DSA in one header is the whole point: the root of trust is mid-migration, carrying both. Firmware signatures are forward-only exposure, but the consequence of a forgery is arbitrary code on a device holding keys, which is why a signer's boot path is where post-quantum signatures matter first even though the spending path is the louder number.

One row, and the only retroactive one here: key agreement in the vendored secp256k1-zkp. Where a shared secret derived through it protects anything stored or recorded, a copy taken today becomes readable once a CRQC exists. Unlike the signature rows it can be hardened without a consensus change, by wrapping the agreed secret under a hybrid KEM.

findings.title: Quantum-vulnerable ECDSA: transaction and message signing (24 file(s))
findings.description: 82 reference(s) to ECDSA across 24 file(s), e.g. vendor/secp256k1-zkp/contrib/lax_der_parsing.c:11. Role, judged from paths, function names and nearby code: transaction and message signing. A CRQC derives the private key from a public key that is already known (on chain after the first spend, in reused addresses): funds and approvals controlled by these keys need a migration path.
findings.impact: Long-term risk depends on what the algorithm protects: signatures (authenticity until migration) or key exchange/encryption (retroactive decryption of recorded data).
findings.recommendation: Follow each chain's post-quantum roadmap, avoid public-key reuse, and keep signers ready to add post-quantum signature schemes as chains adopt them.
findings.limitations: This is a forward-looking risk that depends on the arrival of a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC). No such computer is publicly known to exist today; the timeline is uncertain. It is not a present-day exploitable vulnerability. Heuristic pattern match on source text without data-flow analysis. The usage context (security-relevant or not) must be confirmed manually; treat as preliminary.
findings.method: Regular-expression matching of crypto API patterns; the role comes from words in paths, enclosing function names and the lines around the matches.

quantum_algorithms.name: Shor's algorithm — elliptic-curve discrete logarithms
quantum_algorithms.model_label: Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim
quantum_algorithms.audit: Elliptic-curve keys are expected to fall before RSA keys of comparable classical strength. On blockchains, coins whose public key is already on chain (reused addresses, pay-to-public-key and Taproot outputs) are exposed first; plan the move to post-quantum signatures and avoid key reuse in the meantime.
quantum_algorithms.practicality: 2026 estimates for a 256-bit curve: under 1,200 logical qubits and 90 million Toffoli gates, under half a million physical superconducting qubits running for minutes (Babbush et al.); 1,193 logical qubits with more gates (Chevignard–Fouque–Schrottenloher); P-256 in a few days on 26,000 neutral-atom qubits (Cain et al.). Scenarios under stated assumptions, not forecasts.

quantum_algorithms.name: Grover's algorithm — key search and preimages
quantum_algorithms.model_label: Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim
quantum_algorithms.audit: Not a break. 256-bit keys (AES-256, ChaCha20) keep a comfortable margin; AES-128 meets NIST category 1, while some authorities ask for 256-bit keys in quantum-resistant contexts (see the AES-128 entry). Prefer 256-bit keys for long-lived data; 256-bit hashes need no change for preimage resistance.
quantum_algorithms.practicality: The search is long and serial: NIST counts AES-128 key search as 2^170/MAXDEPTH quantum gates with MAXDEPTH between 2^40 and 2^96 and uses it as the yardstick of security category 1; a SHA-256 preimage was estimated at about 2^153.8 surface-code cycles on 2^12.6 logical qubits (Amy et al. 2016).

quantum_algorithms.name: Brassard–Høyer–Tapp — collision search
quantum_algorithms.model_label: Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim
quantum_algorithms.audit: 256-bit hashes (SHA-256, SHA3-256) remain adequate for collision resistance; 160-bit hashes are already weak classically (SHA-1 collisions are practical). Use 384/512-bit hashes where NIST categories 4–5 are required.
quantum_algorithms.practicality: Bernstein (2009) argued that, once hardware cost is counted, it is not cheaper than classical parallel collision search; NIST defines security category 2 by SHA3-256 collision search counted in classical gates (2^146).

quantum_algorithms.name: Quantum lattice sieving
quantum_algorithms.model_label: Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim
quantum_algorithms.audit: No change for ML-KEM or ML-DSA at the standard parameter sets. A 2024 claim of a polynomial-time quantum LWE algorithm was withdrawn after a bug was found (see claims).
quantum_algorithms.practicality: Needs exponential memory. The Kyber submission sizes its parameters with core-SVP costs of 2^{0.292β} classical and 2^{0.265β} quantum (e.g. 166 quantum bits for Kyber768).

scenario.rationale: Inside the 10-year horizon the survey puts at 28-49% ('quite possible'), and consistent with the BSI estimate of 15 years that 'could shrink to 10 or even less'. Use it for data that must stay confidential for decades, where being wrong is expensive.
